## C01 — Consumer satisfaction measurement program
- Period: 2023-08 to 2026-08
- Role: ANZ Strategy & Planning
- Markets: ANZ
- Skills: survey design, insight synthesis, measurement governance
- Reach out when: You need to build a recurring satisfaction measurement rhythm; You need to translate survey feedback into decision questions
- Trigger: I contributed when teams needed a consistent way to understand changes in consumer satisfaction and the reasons behind them.
- Problem: I needed to help connect a headline advocacy measure with the underlying experiences that could explain movement, while avoiding conclusions unsupported by survey design.
- Method and execution: I helped shape survey questions, organise recurring reviews, and synthesise open-text and structured feedback into themes. I encouraged consistent definitions and cuts over time, highlighted interpretation limits, and framed findings as prompts for further diagnosis rather than direct proof of cause.
- Artifacts: I contributed to survey instruments, measurement workbooks, insight decks, research notes, and an operating cadence.
- Impact and learning: I learned that satisfaction programs are most useful when they combine continuity with room for investigation. The work strengthened a shared capability to interpret consumer feedback carefully and turn broad sentiment into clearer follow-up questions.

- Markets: Australia, New Zealand

- Reach out when: I can help when recurring intelligence needs a clear editorial structure.; I can help make a reporting product easier to sustain and hand over.
- Trigger: I contributed when ANZ stakeholders needed a recurring view of market developments rather than disconnected updates.
- Problem: I helped bring varied market signals into a report that could preserve continuity from one review cycle to the next. The challenge was to provide enough context for interpretation while keeping the product concise, comparable, and maintainable.
- Method and execution: I contributed to gathering inputs, organising themes, checking how claims were framed, and shaping a narrative around what changed and why it might matter. I also helped document the reporting process so the cadence could continue beyond individual contributors.
- Artifacts: I contributed to monthly reports, presentation decks, trackers, briefing notes, and a handover.
- Impact and learning: I learned that recurring reports become decision tools when they use stable questions and editorial standards rather than simply accumulating updates. The work strengthened a reusable reporting capability and made market context easier to carry across planning conversations.

- Skills: market diagnosis, segmentation, strategic synthesis
- Reach out when: A city or category needs a structured growth diagnosis; You need to separate symptoms from addressable constraints
- Trigger: I contributed when uneven growth across cities and categories required a more structured explanation than a single market average.
- Problem: I needed to help identify where performance patterns differed, which constraints might be addressable, and where the available evidence could not support a confident diagnosis.
- Method and execution: I helped break broad questions into comparable city and category views, organised hypotheses around consumer and marketplace conditions, and synthesised findings into a consistent narrative. I separated descriptive evidence from causal interpretation and highlighted where local context changed the meaning of a regional pattern.
- Artifacts: I contributed to diagnostic decks, analytical workbooks, market briefs, and prioritisation notes.
- Impact and learning: I learned that useful diagnosis depends on selecting the right level of detail: broad enough to reveal common patterns, but specific enough to expose local constraints. The work built a reusable structure for moving from uneven outcomes to sharper strategic questions.

## C07 — ANZ membership coverage analysis
- Period: 2023-09 to 2026-07
- Role: ANZ Strategy & Planning
- Markets: ANZ
- Skills: segmentation, diagnostic analysis, strategic synthesis, stakeholder communication
- Reach out when: You need to compare member and non-member experiences; You need a qualitative coverage diagnostic; You need to frame a membership opportunity without exposing restricted metrics
- Trigger: I needed to understand where membership was well represented across the ANZ consumer experience and where the strategic picture remained incomplete.
- Problem: I needed a consistent way to compare member and non-member patterns without reducing the discussion to a single performance measure. The analysis also had to distinguish broad market coverage from differences driven by geography, selection, or consumer behaviour.
- Method and execution: I assembled a structured diagnostic using comparable member and non-member cuts, checked how the story changed across markets and consumer contexts, and translated the findings into decision questions. I focused the narrative on where teams should investigate further, while keeping sensitive performance detail out of general circulation.
- Artifacts: I produced an analysis pack, diagnostic framework, and decision brief.
- Impact and learning: I helped make membership coverage a more interpretable strategy input rather than an isolated reporting cut. I learned that coverage analysis is most useful when it separates availability, relevance, and engagement instead of treating them as the same problem.

- Role: ANZ Strategy & Planning
- Markets: ANZ
- Skills: measurement design, data comparability, research operations, assumption documentation
- Reach out when: I can help when price observations need a defensible comparison method.; I can help document limitations in market measurement.
- Trigger: I contributed when strategy teams needed a consistent way to compare menu and in-store price observations.
- Problem: I worked on the difficulty of comparing prices gathered through different channels, formats, and points in time. The central issue was methodological consistency rather than any individual price point.
- Method and execution: I helped structure a measurement approach, define comparable observations, document exclusions and caveats, and organise repeated collection for analysis. - Impact and learning: I learned that price measurement is most credible when matching rules, timing assumptions, and missing-data treatment are explicit. The work built practical capability for discussing relative positioning while avoiding false precision and keeping limitations visible.

- Skills: launch planning, content governance, cross-functional coordination, risk identification

- Trigger: I needed to plan public product-page updates alongside broader product and customer-communication changes.
- Problem: A webpage update depended on more than drafting text. I needed to reconcile product facts, localization, legal review, implementation ownership, and launch timing while keeping acquisition-facing pages distinct from signed-in customer surfaces.
- Method and execution: I mapped the approval and implementation path, identified which content blocks required specialist support, and sequenced review, preview, and cutover checks. I documented unresolved product and timing questions rather than filling gaps with assumptions. I also distinguished planning readiness from publication, so stakeholders could see what remained before any page change.
- Artifacts: I produced an update plan, review checklist, cutover plan, and ownership map.
- Impact and learning: I created a clearer route from product decision to governed public-page change without claiming delivery ahead of confirmation. I learned that web updates should be treated as small launches, with explicit owners for facts, language, implementation, and timing.

## C30 — Localising a global engagement-benefit concept
- Period: 2026
- Role: Regional Membership Strategy (APAC)
- Markets: Multi-market
- Skills: concept localisation, usage-based modelling, assumption management, scope control
- Reach out when: You need to adapt a global loyalty mechanic to a market with different behaviour; You need a directional cost model before a finance model exists
- Trigger: A globally designed engagement-benefit concept needed to be assessed for markets with different member behaviour and economics.
- Problem: I had to avoid copying another market's parameters. The design needed to reward engagement, constrain cost exposure, and stay useful even if the full product experience was delayed.
- Method and execution: I derived member segments, qualification cuts, and redemption behaviour from local usage patterns rather than transplanted assumptions. I kept optional and premium benefits costed separately from the core mechanic, documented every adjustable assumption, and made a fallback using existing tools an explicit decision rather than an afterthought.
- Artifacts: I produced decision frameworks, a cost simulator, validation checks, and an assumption register.
- Impact and learning: I learned that regional reuse should preserve modelling discipline, not transplant parameters, and that premium benefits should be costed and approved independently of the core design.

## C31 — Benefit economics and funding discipline
- Period: 2026
- Role: Regional Membership Strategy (APAC)
- Markets: Multi-market
- Skills: economic modelling, cost-control design, sensitivity framing, trade-off communication
- Reach out when: You need to redirect diffuse discount spend into a benefit members understand; A benefit risks concentrating spend on already-loyal users
- Trigger: Benefit proposals needed a clearer account of what they cost, what they replaced, and who would consume them.
- Problem: I needed to make funding logic legible without claiming new benefits were cost-neutral, and to stop cost scaling mechanically with the heaviest users.
- Method and execution: I modelled reallocation of existing spend as a distinct lever and showed freed spend alongside gross cost. For heavy-usage risk I translated the problem into product levers such as delayed eligibility, value adjustments, exposure caps, and basket conditions, and compared them against behaviour at the tail. When data sources disagreed, I kept the gap visible rather than forcing agreement.
- Artifacts: I built funding controls into decision simulators and produced cost sensitivities and governance checklists.
- Impact and learning: I learned that funding claims need the same source and population discipline as customer metrics, and that good benefits reward incremental behaviour rather than subsidising what would happen anyway.

## C32 — Framing recurring-benefit experiments
- Period: 2026
- Role: Regional Membership Strategy (APAC)
- Markets: Multi-market
- Skills: experiment design, treatment separation, launch risk assessment, measurement framing
- Reach out when: You need to test a simple recurring member benefit cleanly; Several benefit ideas risk being tested as one bundle
- Trigger: Several candidate member benefits were being explored at the same time.
- Problem: I needed to keep distinct mechanics from being confused with one another, and to stop an attractive but immature capability becoming a dependency for the core roadmap.
- Method and execution: I clarified what each benefit did and did not test, helped structure separate and combined treatments, and pushed for clean controls when adjacent treatments were not ready. I treated early production ramps as readiness evidence only, not proof of customer impact.
- Artifacts: I developed decision briefs, treatment comparisons, readiness checks, and a measurement agenda.
- Impact and learning: I learned that simple customer mechanics still need careful enrolment, scope, and evidence governance, and that decoupling adjacent ideas lets the core roadmap move independently.

## C33 — Measuring membership price and benefit changes
- Period: 2026
- Role: Regional Membership Strategy (APAC)
- Markets: Multi-market
- Skills: cohort design, measurement governance, metric reconciliation, cross-market synthesis
- Reach out when: You are planning a membership repricing; You need to separate launch health from mature retention
- Trigger: Membership price and benefit changes needed an evaluation method that would hold up as evidence matured.
- Problem: Announcement reactions, new-member acquisition, and existing-member renewals happen on different clocks. Early signals are useful but cannot answer the retention question before renewals mature, and monthly and annual plans behave differently.
- Method and execution: I structured analysis around customer events rather than a single launch date, separating notices, opt-outs, starts, active and passive churn, and renewal-aligned retention, with annual plans measured independently. I required readouts to label immature cohorts rather than treating missing renewals as churn, reconciled sources and disclosed differences, and turned the lessons into a reusable playbook.
- Artifacts: I contributed measurement requirements, metric definitions, readiness checklists, and a cross-market playbook.
- Impact and learning: I learned to measure customers at their actual renewal boundary: early acquisition can look resilient while cancellation risk is still delayed.

## C34 — Acquisition offer portfolio design
- Period: 2026
- Role: Regional Membership Strategy (APAC)
- Markets: Multi-market
- Skills: portfolio strategy, cohort analysis, decision framing, scenario analysis
- Reach out when: You need to choose between free trials, discounted months, and annual offers; Member growth and paid conversion point in different directions
- Trigger: Acquisition offers needed to be judged on quality of conversion, not just the number of starts.
- Problem: Longer free access can lift starts while delaying the point at which willingness to pay becomes observable. Promotional demand also needed to be separated from underlying plan demand.
- Method and execution: I compared offer structures (free trials, trial-plus-discount bundles, discounted annual commitments) against an explicit objective hierarchy, segmented decisions by membership history and engagement, and checked that live configuration matched strategic intent.
- Artifacts: I produced offer reviews, cohort decision matrices, measurement frameworks, and readiness checklists.
- Impact and learning: I learned to declare the primary objective before optimising offer duration: member stock, paid members, and long-term value can point to different decisions at the same time.

## C35 — Lifecycle targeting for membership offers
- Period: 2026
- Role: Regional Membership Strategy (APAC)
- Markets: Multi-market
- Skills: segmentation strategy, model translation, risk framing, requirements
- Reach out when: You need to replace blanket offers with lifecycle logic; You need to assess whether a model built elsewhere transfers to your market
- Trigger: Offers were being shown to broad audiences without accounting for membership history or engagement.
- Problem: Audiences that are broad or change abruptly make it hard to tell whether movement came from demand, targeting, or operations. Models built for other markets also needed a portability check.
- Method and execution: I translated diagnostics into targeting rules based on prior membership, activity, and likely retention value, and defined questions on audience refresh, exclusions, and offer conflicts. For externally built allocation models I documented assumptions and mapped which local conditions could invalidate transfer.
- Artifacts: I produced targeting frameworks, readiness gates, model-assumption reviews, and a market-fit matrix.
- Impact and learning: I learned that personalisation only creates value when assignment logic and measurement populations stay traceable, and that model portability depends on local economics as much as predictive accuracy.

## C36 — Retention and win-back portfolio
- Period: 2026
- Role: Regional Membership Strategy (APAC)
- Markets: Multi-market
- Skills: retention strategy, portfolio design, holdout governance, rollout coordination
- Reach out when: You need a structured response to cancellation intent; You need to recover former paid members without blanket discounts
- Trigger: Members showing cancellation intent, and recently lapsed paid members, needed a more structured response than one universal discount.
- Problem: A single rescue offer hides real differences between plan types and preferences, and results cannot be read without proven configuration and credible holdouts.
- Method and execution: I framed retention as a portfolio of testable mechanics (pre-renewal engagement goals, plan and benefit offers, time-bound return incentives) and separated cancellation intent from realised churn. I checked approved designs against verified production state and defined holdout requirements before any recovery was attributed.
- Artifacts: I produced portfolio summaries, configuration checklists, measurement briefs, and handover views.
- Impact and learning: I learned that configuration completeness and holdout validity must be proven before claiming recovery, and that win-back mechanics need a precise definition of eligible history.

## C37 — Engagement quest design and exposure integrity
- Period: 2026
- Role: Regional Membership Strategy (APAC)
- Markets: Multi-market
- Skills: cohort strategy, experiment deconfliction, targeting, scaling criteria
- Reach out when: You are designing goal-based incentives; Concurrent campaigns may contaminate controls; A global programme needs market-level decisions
- Trigger: Goal-based incentives (quests) were being used to stretch habits and encourage cross-product use.
- Problem: Broad targeting risks paying for behaviour that would happen anyway, delayed audience loading makes nominal start dates unreliable, and overlapping campaigns can contaminate comparison groups.
- Method and execution: I reframed readiness around the first verified customer exposure, required protection for treated and comparison cohorts, documented precedence across overlapping campaigns, and argued for excluding customers likely to act organically. I kept engagement learning separate from retention claims.
- Artifacts: I produced portfolio assessments, an exposure-integrity framework, readiness checklists, and risk registers.
- Impact and learning: I learned to version cohort snapshots, record first exposure, reconcile issued and redeemed rewards, and delay scaling until each cohort has a clean, mature observation window.

## C38 — Self-service campaign tracking and spend estimation
- Period: 2026
- Role: Regional Membership Strategy (APAC)
- Markets: Multi-market
- Skills: product requirements, workflow design, measurement governance
- Reach out when: Local teams lack campaign visibility; Incentive spend is hard to estimate
- Trigger: Local teams relied on central operators to understand campaign exposure, progress, and likely spend.
- Problem: A self-service tool needed to add transparency without false precision, especially when data delays and overlapping campaigns made nominal data unreliable.
- Method and execution: I framed a tracking and estimation workflow around operating decisions rather than dashboard volume, emphasising exposure timestamps, configurable assumptions, and a clear split between approved budget, projected issuance, redemption, and realised cost.
- Artifacts: I contributed requirements, data definitions, and a local-operations workflow.
- Impact and learning: I learned that trustworthy tools must expose data freshness and assumption boundaries, or they automate the same ambiguity that slowed manual work.

## C39 — Regional participation decisions for global features
- Period: 2026
- Role: Regional Membership Strategy (APAC)
- Markets: Multi-market
- Skills: opt-in governance, economic framing, capability assessment, experiment readiness
- Reach out when: A global feature needs differentiated market decisions; Market applicability differs across a region
- Trigger: Globally designed member features needed explicit decisions about where regional participation made sense.
- Problem: Markets differ in demand patterns, commercial structure, regulation, and ability to run readable tests, so a blanket regional response would be wrong.
- Method and execution: I coordinated explicit market participation decisions based on applicability, learning value, cost tolerance, and concurrent changes. I challenged stale status labels, separated modelled exposure from observed outcomes, and required experiment plans and decision rules before scaling. For partner-funded offers, I turned manual campaign patterns into product and measurement requirements.
- Artifacts: I produced decision briefs, applicability matrices, capability assessments, and readiness gates.
- Impact and learning: I learned that an affordable test is not automatically informative, and that a local success does not prove viability across a whole market.

## C40 — Benefit simplification and customer comprehension
- Period: 2026
- Role: Regional Membership Strategy (APAC)
- Markets: Multi-market
- Skills: strategic framing, customer comprehension, guardrail design, readiness governance
- Reach out when: Members struggle to understand a benefit; You need a value-neutral redesign with clear guardrails
- Trigger: Some member value was real but hard for customers to recognise and explain.
- Problem: Complex discounts can make value feel opaque. Simplifying a benefit, or using it to encourage use of another product, has to be economically controlled and must not be presented as an automatic value increase.
- Method and execution: I framed benefit redesign around whether customers understand and attribute value, not just whether the economics balance. I set guardrails on the overall benefit envelope and asked product, finance, and legal partners to validate feasibility, customer language, and measurement before any commitment.
- Artifacts: I produced customer-value framing, decision questions, and dependency lists.
- Impact and learning: I learned that value-neutral on paper is not launch-ready: serving, comprehension, customer copy, assignment, and measurement each need independent proof.

## C41 — Release gates for benefit-platform and public-page changes
- Period: 2026
- Role: Regional Membership Strategy (APAC)
- Markets: Multi-market
- Skills: migration governance, content governance, test planning, risk escalation
- Reach out when: A platform migration depends on dynamic testing; A public page must reflect a product change accurately
- Trigger: Benefit-platform changes and public product pages needed to stay aligned with what customers actually experience.
- Problem: Entering configuration does not prove offers will serve correctly, and a correct draft page is not enough when different customer groups change on different schedules.
- Method and execution: I separated static configuration from dynamic proof and held release to named test owners, production evidence, and defect accountability. For public pages I mapped the review chain, protected unconfirmed content from accidental publication, and required localised previews before scheduling.
- Artifacts: I produced test-evidence requirements, hold-or-release gates, reviewer maps, and pre-publication checklists.
- Impact and learning: I learned that completeness must be measured through observed customer states, and that public-page updates should be run as small launches with explicit owners.

## C42 — Eligibility-verification capacity planning
- Period: 2026
- Role: Regional Membership Strategy (APAC)
- Markets: Multi-market
- Skills: forecasting, requirements gathering, risk management
- Reach out when: You need to connect eligibility demand with operational capacity; You need to avoid decisions based on stale utilisation
- Trigger: Eligibility verification for a member segment was both a customer-access mechanic and an operational capacity constraint.
- Problem: Forecasts existed, but current utilisation and verification performance needed reconciling before any capacity decision.
- Method and execution: I assembled demand inputs, defined forecasting approaches for growing and declining segments, and withheld recommendations until current utilisation was confirmed.
- Artifacts: I produced a capacity tracker, forecast structure, and decision framework.
- Impact and learning: I learned that entitlement planning must combine demand, conversion, utilisation, and operational mechanics rather than extrapolating from member counts alone.

## C43 — ANZ strategy and planning role handover
- Period: 2026-02 to 2026-07
- Role: ANZ Strategy & Planning
- Markets: ANZ
- Skills: knowledge transfer, documentation, stakeholder mapping, workstream prioritisation
- Reach out when: You are planning a role transition; You need to turn a broad remit into a usable handover; You need continuity across recurring strategy work
- Trigger: I was moving from an ANZ strategy and planning role into a regional consumer role and needed to leave the work in a usable state.
- Problem: I needed to transfer more than a list of open tasks. The incoming owner needed context on recurring decisions, stakeholder expectations, analytical assets, and the difference between ongoing operating work and questions that still required judgment.
- Method and execution: I organised the remit by workstream, documented purpose and cadence, separated completed work from open decisions, and created an inventory of the reporting and analysis surfaces used by the team. I also highlighted dependencies, practical access needs, and areas where a new owner should revalidate assumptions rather than inherit them unchanged.
- Artifacts: I produced a handover, workstream inventory, dashboard inventory, and transition checklist.
- Impact and learning: I made the transition easier to navigate and reduced reliance on informal context. The lasting lesson was that a useful handover should explain how decisions get made, not simply where files are stored.

## C44 — Fuel-cost signals and consumer behaviour
- Period: 2026-03 to 2026-08
- Role: ANZ Strategy & Planning
- Markets: ANZ
- Skills: hypothesis framing, signal interpretation, research synthesis
- Reach out when: you need to translate an external signal into consumer questions; you want a method-first view of a market change
- Trigger: I contributed when changing fuel costs raised questions about how consumers might adjust their behaviour across mobility and delivery.
- Problem: I was helping turn a visible external signal into a careful set of behavioural hypotheses without assuming that timing alone demonstrated a causal relationship.
- Method and execution: I supported a structured review of the signal, mapped plausible consumer responses, and distinguished immediate observations from questions requiring deeper validation. I treated alternative explanations as part of the analysis and kept the framing broad enough to connect market context with operational data later.
- Artifacts: Research note and signal tracker.
- Impact and learning: I learned that macro signals are valuable prompts but weak conclusions on their own. The durable method is to state the behavioural pathway explicitly, identify competing explanations, and define what evidence would meaningfully change the interpretation.

## C45 — Promotional-response analysis
- Period: 2026-04 to 2026-09
- Role: ANZ Strategy & Planning
- Markets: Australia
- Skills: cohort analysis, scenario framing, monitoring design
- Reach out when: A competitor promotion needs a measured response; You need cohort-level monitoring before escalating action
- Trigger: I contributed when a major competitor promotion raised questions about customer exposure and the appropriate level of response.
- Problem: I needed to help distinguish immediate competitive pressure from normal variation, while showing which customer groups and experience components warranted closer attention.
- Method and execution: I developed analytical cuts across customer behaviour, segmented exposure into decision-relevant cohorts, and helped frame response options with explicit trade-offs. I also helped define a monitoring approach that separated routine observation from conditions that would justify escalation, while keeping open risks visible for leadership discussion.
- Artifacts: I produced analytical readouts, a cohort framework, a scenario model, a monitoring specification, and a leadership deck.
- Impact and learning: I learned that a credible response does not require immediate broad action. Combining cohort-level evidence, explicit thresholds, and clear caveats created a more disciplined way to monitor the situation and discuss proportionate options.

## C46 — Membership product and operations collaboration cadence
- Period: 2026-04 to 2026-09
- Role: APAC Membership
- Markets: APAC
- Skills: cross-functional facilitation, agenda design, dependency management, follow-through
- Reach out when: You need a useful product and operations rhythm; Dependencies are getting lost between teams; A recurring meeting needs clearer decisions and follow-through
- Trigger: I needed a dependable way for regional operations and product partners to review membership dependencies and decisions.
- Problem: Important updates were spread across separate workstreams, and recurring meetings could easily become status exchanges without clear decisions. I needed a rhythm that made ownership, escalation needs, and follow-up visible while respecting the different responsibilities of product and operations teams.
- Method and execution: I helped shape a recurring agenda around decisions, dependencies, launches, and unresolved questions. I brought structured pre-reads, clarified the requested outcome for each topic, and captured owners and next steps. I also carried market context into the forum and returned product guidance to the relevant operating teams.
- Artifacts: I produced an operating cadence, agenda template, decision log, and action tracker.
- Impact and learning: I helped turn cross-functional updates into a more decision-oriented working rhythm. I learned that these forums are most effective when every agenda item names the decision or dependency it is intended to resolve.

## C47 — APAC consumer strategy role and dashboard kickoff
- Period: 2026-04 to 2026-09
- Role: APAC Consumer Strategy
- Markets: Multi-market
- Skills: role design, operating-model design, dashboard scoping, metric governance, prototyping
- Reach out when: You are defining a new regional strategy remit; You need to scope a dashboard before building it; You need to reconcile global definitions with local reporting
- Trigger: I entered a newly created APAC consumer strategy remit and needed to define both the role and its first decision-support workstream.
- Problem: The remit was intentionally broad, and existing global and market reporting did not yet provide one comparable regional consumer view. I needed to clarify where regional strategy should coordinate, where it should provide frameworks, and where ownership should remain with product, market, or specialist teams.
- Method and execution: I researched adjacent operating models, drafted role boundaries and decision responsibilities, surveyed existing dashboards, and mapped candidate metrics to their governance status. I then created a phased consultation and build plan plus a synthetic-data mockup to test information architecture, filters, cadence, and drill-down behavior before any production build.
- Artifacts: I produced a role-scope proposal, responsibility framework, metric catalog, dashboard plan, and prototype.
- Impact and learning: I established a concrete kickoff for role-design and dashboard-planning discussions; I did not deliver the production dashboard. The main learning was to settle decision ownership and metric governance before investing in implementation.

## C48 — Market membership priority alignment
- Period: 2026-06 to 2026-09
- Role: APAC Membership
- Markets: APAC
- Skills: facilitation, requirements synthesis, prioritisation, decision framing
- Reach out when: You need to reconcile regional and market priorities; You need a clear pre-read for a planning discussion; You need to expose unresolved assumptions before escalation
- Trigger: I needed to align market membership priorities before they entered regional planning and product conversations.
- Problem: Markets described needs at different levels of detail and with different assumptions about timing, ownership, and supporting evidence. I needed to preserve local context while making the requests comparable enough for a regional discussion.
- Method and execution: I translated market inputs into a common structure covering the user problem, decision required, dependency, maturity, and owner. I separated confirmed needs from hypotheses, surfaced conflicts and missing evidence, and used working sessions to refine the framing. Where alignment was not possible, I recorded the decision gap rather than forcing consensus.
- Artifacts: I produced an alignment brief, prioritisation template, decision log, and workshop pre-read.
- Impact and learning: I helped regional and market stakeholders discuss priorities from the same starting point. I learned that alignment is not agreement on every item; it is shared clarity on what is known, what remains disputed, and who should decide next.

## C49 — APAC competitive-intelligence capability matrix
- Period: 2026-07 to 2026-09
- Role: APAC Membership
- Markets: Multi-market
- Skills: capability mapping, evidence assessment, taxonomy design, prioritisation
- Reach out when: You need to compare intelligence capabilities across markets; You need an evidence-aware capability assessment; You need to turn scattered research assets into a regional operating view
- Trigger: I needed to understand how consistently competitive intelligence could support consumer and membership decisions across APAC markets.
- Problem: Markets had different research assets, definitions, cadences, and evidence quality. I needed a comparable view that showed where a capability existed, how dependable it was, and what should be strengthened, without presenting incomplete coverage as absence.
- Method and execution: I defined a common capability taxonomy, normalized market inputs, and separated verified evidence from reported or unresolved coverage. I grouped related capabilities into clear domains, recorded freshness and quality caveats, and created a prioritisation view for next steps. I preserved local nuance while making the regional comparison easy to scan.
- Artifacts: I produced a capability matrix, evidence register, taxonomy, and prioritisation view.
- Impact and learning: I created a shared baseline for discussing intelligence capability and investment needs across markets. I learned that a useful maturity view must show evidence quality and recency, not just assign a status.
